claims.text: Elevated-temperature microscopic deformation of FeNiCrCoCu is governed by its near-surface microstructure.
The overall sliding-wear resistance of a FeNiCrCoCu coating is governed by its near-surface microstructure.
A finer, more equiaxed grain structure has a higher grain-boundary density.
The increased grain-boundary density of the refined coating impedes thermally activated dislocation motion.
Grain refinement delays dynamic recovery and recrystallization during high-temperature sliding.
Impeded dislocation motion and delayed recovery reduce microscopic plastic deformation.
Reduced microscopic plastic deformation lowers the wear of the FeNiCrCoCu coating.
A coarser microstructure permits dislocation pile-ups and localized slip during sliding.
Dislocation pile-ups and localized slip in a coarser coating increase wear.
Conventional deposition conditions produce a baseline FeNiCrCoCu coating with relatively coarse or moderate grains.
Increasing the deposition cooling rate will produce a finer and more uniformly equiaxed FeNiCrCoCu coating microstructure.
At approximately 700–1073 K, thermally activated dislocation processes and dynamic recovery become significant in the coating.
A refined grain structure reduces dislocation glide and localized slip-band formation during elevated-temperature sliding.
A refined grain structure minimizes adhesive and abrasive wear.
The refined coating will have a lower average friction coefficient than the baseline coating under identical high-temperature sliding conditions.
The refined coating will have a lower wear rate than the baseline coating under identical high-temperature sliding conditions.
The refined coating will exhibit fewer dislocation pile-ups or concentrated slip bands than the baseline coating.
The proposed mechanism applies above about 700 K but ceases to govern once complete softening or oxidation-driven wear dominates.
